focus: Section 2 Algorithm 1 and Section 3 (initialization bias correction) of Adam. Explain how Adam keeps exponential moving averages of the gradient (m) and squared gradient (v), why they are biased toward zero at the start, and how dividing by (1 - beta^t) corrects this. Use a short sequence of scalar gradients the learner can edit, with sliders for beta1, beta2 and the step size alpha. Show m, v, the bias-corrected m_hat, v_hat and the parameter update at each step. Guide the learner through constant gradients (bias correction gives exactly the gradient) and a sign-flipping gradient. Check that m_hat equals g for constant gradient g and that the effective step magnitude stays near alpha.
audience: engineering undergraduate familiar with gradient descent
excerpt: Algorithm 1 (paraphrased): Adam. Good default settings are alpha = 0.001, beta1 = 0.9, beta2 = 0.999 and epsilon = 1e-8. Initialize m_0 = 0, v_0 = 0, t = 0. While not converged: t = t + 1; g_t = gradient of the objective at theta_{t-1}; m_t = beta1 * m_{t-1} + (1 - beta1) * g_t (update biased first moment estimate); v_t = beta2 * v_{t-1} + (1 - beta2) * g_t^2 (update biased second raw moment estimate); m_hat_t = m_t / (1 - beta1^t) (bias-corrected first moment); v_hat_t = v_t / (1 - beta2^t) (bias-corrected second moment); theta_t = theta_{t-1} - alpha * m_hat_t / (sqrt(v_hat_t) + epsilon). Section 2.1: the effective step is Delta_t = alpha * m_hat_t / sqrt(v_hat_t); its magnitude is approximately bounded by the stepsize alpha. Section 3 (paraphrased): because the moving averages are initialized as vectors of zeros, they are biased towards zero, especially during the initial timesteps and when the decay rates are small (betas close to 1). If the true second moment is stationary, E[v_t] = E[g_t^2] * (1 - beta2^t), so dividing by (1 - beta2^t) corrects the initialization bias; the same holds for the first moment.
